content: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding refers to the loss of blood from any part of the gastrointestinal tract, which extends from the mouth to the anus. It is also known as gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Depending on the site of origin, GI bleeding is classified into two categories: upper gastrointestinal bleeding (UGIB) and lower gastrointestinal bleeding (LGIB). Upper gastrointestinal bleeding is defined as bleeding that originates proximal to the ligament of Treitz, which is located at the junction of the duodenum and jejunum. The most common causes of UGIB include peptic ulcer disease and esophageal varices. Lower gastrointestinal bleeding, on the other hand, refers to blood loss originating distal to the ligament of Treitz, with diverticulosis being the most frequent cause. The clinical presentation of GI bleeding can vary. Overt bleeding may manifest as hematemesis, which is the vomiting of fresh red blood, or as coffee ground emesis, which is the vomiting of altered black blood. It may also present as melena, characterized by the passage of black, tarry stools, or as hematochezia, which is the passage of bright red blood per rectum. Hematochezia is typically associated with lower GI bleeding but can also occur in cases of massive upper GI bleeding. Rebleeding should always be confirmed through endoscopy. Several risk factors contribute to the development of GI bleeding. These include advanced age, a prior history of gastrointestinal bleeding, chronic constipation, hematologic disorders, and the use of medications such as anticoagulants and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). It is crucial to differentiate between lower GI bleeding and brisk upper GI bleeding, as they can present with similar symptoms. Patients experiencing severe bleeding or hemodynamic instability require hospitalization and urgent diagnostic evaluation. The treatment approach depends on the underlying cause and the severity of the bleeding.
